plan.taskTitle: Write a 10-page paper on the causes of WWI by Friday
plan.analysis: With only three days, the plan compresses roughly 11 hours of work into short sessions across Wednesday to Friday, separating ugly drafting from polishing and giving each step a hard stopping point.

steps.title: Open the doc and paste in the prompt
steps.description: Create a new doc named 'WWI paper', paste in the assignment prompt and the due date, and type 'UGLY FIRST DRAFT' at the top. Done when the doc is saved and open.

steps.title: Gather 5-6 sources
steps.description: Skim your textbook chapter on WWI and use your library database to find 5 or 6 sources, such as Christopher Clark's The Sleepwalkers or Margaret MacMillan's The War That Ended Peace. Paste the links or citations into the doc and stop; you do not need to read them all yet.

steps.title: Take messy notes on the MAIN causes
steps.description: Read and skim your sources for militarism, alliances, imperialism, nationalism, and the July Crisis after the assassination of Franz Ferdinand. Write rough bullet points under each heading with page numbers; typos and fragments are fine. Stop at 60 minutes even if you feel unfinished.

steps.title: Write a bullet-point outline with a thesis
steps.description: Turn your notes into a rough outline: one sentence for your thesis, then 4-5 body sections with 2-3 bullets each. A weak thesis is fine because you can fix it later. Stop when every section has bullets.

steps.title: Ugly draft: intro and alliances/militarism sections
steps.description: Write about 4 pages covering your intro and the first two body sections, following your outline. Do not edit or delete anything while you write; stop when you hit about 4 pages or the timer runs out.

steps.title: Ugly draft: imperialism and nationalism sections
steps.description: Write about 3 pages on imperialism and nationalism, including the Balkans. Keep going even when sentences are clumsy, and put [FIX] in brackets where you are stuck. Stop at about 3 pages.

steps.title: Ugly draft: July Crisis and conclusion
steps.description: Write about 3 pages on the July Crisis plus your conclusion, which restates your thesis. Once you reach the end of the conclusion, the first complete draft exists and you are done for this step.

steps.title: Fill gaps and check the length
steps.description: Go through every [FIX] note and fill it with a rough sentence or a quote and citation. Check that you are at or near 10 pages, and add or trim a paragraph if not. Stop once no [FIX] notes remain.

steps.title: Polish pass: structure and thesis
steps.description: Read through once and tweak only your thesis, topic sentences, and paragraph order. Do not touch word choice yet. Stop after one pass through the whole paper.

steps.title: Polish pass: citations, proofread, and submit
steps.description: Format your citations and bibliography, run spell-check, skim for typos, and submit. Good enough is the goal, and one pass is the limit. Done when it is submitted.

grade.notes: Step 14 (flashcard run-through) is scheduled 'Tonight' but placed last, so it appears after Monday's steps and logically belongs on Monday night; Step 3 is also 'Tonight' right after step 2 'Today', creating a heavy first day and a Thursday/Saturday/Sunday/Monday load of 90+ min blocks. Step 2 says '5 headings' but chapters 5-9 could be fine, yet sessions are 45 min blocks that are not very small for an overwhelmed student, and the reassurance is thin and repetitive.

plan.taskTitle: Study for organic chemistry midterm (chapters 5-9)
plan.analysis: Spread about 11 hours of small, standalone sessions across the days to Tuesday, one chapter at a time, then practice problems and a final review, finishing by Monday.

steps.title: Set out your materials
steps.description: Put your o-chem textbook and notebook on your desk, open to chapter 5. That's it, you're done.

steps.title: List the chapter 5-9 topics
steps.description: Copy the chapter titles from the textbook contents page onto one sheet of paper. Done when you have 5 headings written down.

steps.title: Review chapter 5 notes
steps.description: Skim your chapter 5 notes and highlight the key reactions and mechanisms. Stop when you reach the end of the chapter.

steps.title: Chapter 5 practice problems
steps.description: Do the end-of-chapter problems for chapter 5, checking answers as you go. Mark any you missed with a star.

steps.title: Review chapter 6 notes
steps.description: Skim your chapter 6 notes and write the key reactions on flashcards. This session stands alone, so don't worry about the other chapters.

steps.title: Chapter 6 practice problems
steps.description: Work the chapter 6 end-of-chapter problems and star the ones you miss.

steps.title: Review chapter 7 notes
steps.description: Skim your chapter 7 notes and make flashcards for the main mechanisms. Done when each mechanism has a card.

steps.title: Chapter 7 practice problems
steps.description: Do the chapter 7 end-of-chapter problems and star the ones you miss.

steps.title: Review chapter 8 notes
steps.description: Skim your chapter 8 notes and write out the key reactions on flashcards. One chapter only, nothing more today.

steps.title: Chapter 8 practice problems
steps.description: Work the chapter 8 end-of-chapter problems and star the ones you miss.

steps.title: Review chapter 9 notes
steps.description: Skim your chapter 9 notes and make flashcards for the key reactions. You're nearly through the material.

steps.title: Chapter 9 practice problems
steps.description: Do the chapter 9 end-of-chapter problems and star the ones you miss.

steps.title: Redo starred problems
steps.description: Go back through every starred problem from chapters 5-9 and redo it without looking at the answer. Done when you've attempted them all.

steps.title: Flashcard run-through
steps.description: Go through all your flashcards once, setting aside the ones you miss. Re-read those a final time.

grade.notes: Steps are generic to any problem set (no calc-specific cues like reviewing the relevant section or a worked example first), and timing is vague ('Tonight', 'Tomorrow' with no times, unclear deadline hour) so tomorrow's 90 minutes could collide with class; the first step also still asks the student to gather several items.

plan.taskTitle: Finish calc problem set 4 (all 12 problems)
plan.analysis: With only today and tomorrow, we'll start with a tiny setup step, then split the 12 problems into three gentle chunks of four, with a final check tomorrow before it's due.

steps.title: Just set up your workspace
steps.description: Just open the problem set and your textbook or notes, and put a pencil and some scratch paper next to them. Done means everything is on your desk, and you don't have to solve anything yet.

steps.title: Just try problems 1-4
steps.description: Just work through problems 1-4 and write down whatever you can, even if it's messy. If one stumps you, put a star next to it and move on; done means all four have at least an attempt.

steps.title: Just try problems 5-8
steps.description: Take a short break, then just work through problems 5-8 the same way, starring any that feel stuck. Done means every one of them has an attempt on paper.

steps.title: Just try problems 9-12
steps.description: Just give problems 9-12 a go with the same star-and-move-on approach. Done means all 12 problems have something written down.

steps.title: Just revisit your starred problems
steps.description: Just look back at the starred problems, check your notes or textbook examples for similar ones, and try again. If one is still stuck, jot down your best attempt or a question to ask your professor or TA.

steps.title: Just tidy up and submit
steps.description: Just skim through all 12 answers, make sure your work is legible and each problem is labeled, then submit or pack it up for class. Done means it's handed in or in your bag.

grade.notes: Step 1 says "five column headers" but lists only four, and it asks for a decision about doc vs. spreadsheet. Step 2 on the same day is a 30-minute browsing task that is hard for an avoider. Also, Oct 14 is the day before the deadline, so the last application and the check should have more buffer, and the "Just..." phrasing is repetitive.

plan.taskTitle: Apply to 5 software engineering summer internships
plan.analysis: Start with a tiny setup action, then build one reusable resume and application kit, and apply to one internship at a time spread evenly through Oct 15, finishing a day early.

steps.title: Open a tracker doc
steps.description: Just create a new doc or spreadsheet called 'Internship Apps' and type the five column headers: Company, Link, Deadline, Status. That's it, you're done.

steps.title: Gather 8 listings you might like
steps.description: Just open your school career portal, LinkedIn, or a internship listings page and paste the links of 8 software engineering internships into your tracker. Don't judge them yet, just collect.

steps.title: Pick your 5 and note their deadlines
steps.description: Just look at your 8 links and star the 5 that feel least scary, favoring ones with earlier deadlines. Write each deadline in the tracker and you're done.

steps.title: Dust off your resume
steps.description: Just open your current resume (or a template if you don't have one) and update it with your latest courses, projects, and any job. Rough is fine, it just needs to be current.

steps.title: Tighten the project bullets
steps.description: Just rewrite the bullets for your top 2-3 projects so each says what you built, the tech you used, and one result. Save it as a PDF when finished.

steps.title: Write a reusable cover letter draft
steps.description: Just write a 3-paragraph template: why you like software engineering, one project you're proud of, and a blank line for company-specific details. A rough draft is totally fine.

steps.title: Apply to internship #1
steps.description: Just fill in the first application using your resume and template, customizing one sentence in the cover letter. Submit it and mark it 'Applied' in your tracker.

steps.title: Apply to internship #2
steps.description: Just do the second one the same way. Reusing your materials makes it faster, so submit it and update your tracker.

steps.title: Apply to internship #3
steps.description: Just submit one more application, tweaking a sentence or two of your cover letter. Mark it done in your tracker.

steps.title: Apply to internship #4
steps.description: Just handle the fourth application, then give yourself a little break, since you're most of the way there.

steps.title: Apply to internship #5
steps.description: Just submit your last application and update the tracker. Five applications sent, nicely done.

steps.title: Quick check of your confirmations
steps.description: Just glance through your email for the five confirmation messages and mark each as confirmed in your tracker. If one's missing, make a note to follow up.

grade.notes: Step 8 (closet/drawer tidy) is placed after the final walkthrough and photo, so the 'done' moment comes before the last task; Saturday is also overloaded with four steps. The first step is small but still involves a walk-through and a trash bag, and the boredom adaptation is good (timers, playlist, challenges) but could be more varied or game-like.

plan.taskTitle: Clean my room by Sunday
plan.analysis: Split the cleanup into short, timeboxed, varied sessions spread from today through Saturday so the room is done a day before the Sunday deadline.

steps.title: Grab a trash bag and do a 3-minute sweep
steps.description: Get one trash bag and walk your room once, tossing only obvious trash (wrappers, old receipts, empty bottles). Done when the bag is tied and by your door.

steps.title: Laundry round-up
steps.description: Set a 15-minute timer and gather every piece of clothing from the floor, chair, and bed into a hamper or laundry basket; hang up anything clean. Done when no clothes are visible outside the closet or hamper.

steps.title: Dishes and cups mission
steps.description: Collect every cup, plate, and bowl in your room and carry them to the kitchen in one trip, challenge: beat 10 minutes. Done when no dishes remain in your room.

steps.title: Clear your desk
steps.description: Set a 25-minute timer and put on a playlist. Sort everything on your desk into keep, relocate, or toss piles, then put each pile where it belongs and leave only what you use daily. Done when the desk surface is visible.

steps.title: Bed and floor reset
steps.description: Strip and remake your bed (start the sheets in the wash), then gather leftover floor items into one box and put each away. Set a 25-minute timer; done when you can see all the floor.

steps.title: Dust and vacuum power round
steps.description: Set a 25-minute timer: wipe the desk, nightstand, and shelves with a damp cloth, then vacuum the whole floor, finishing at the door. Done when the vacuum has covered every corner.

steps.title: Final walkthrough and photo
steps.description: Spend 10 minutes fixing any leftover spots, take out the trash bag, and snap an after photo from the doorway. Done when you could comfortably invite a friend in.

steps.title: Quick closet and drawer tidy
steps.description: Set a 15-minute timer and refold or rehang what's messy in one drawer and your closet, bagging any clothes you want to donate. Done when the bag is by the door and the drawers shut easily.

grade.notes: The first step is concrete but mixes creating the deck with messaging the group (and writing a message), which is slightly more than a pure tiny action. Sequence is weaker: sources are gathered after slides are assigned but before building, and 'first half' vs 'remaining slides' is vague for a group project. Everything is fitted into one Sunday review block with no buffer for late teammates.

plan.taskTitle: Finish 10-slide Tesla marketing strategy deck for Business 101
plan.analysis: Group project with a Monday 9am deadline, so spread about 6 hours of work across Wed-Sun, starting with a tiny setup action, coordinating the group early, and leaving Sunday for a final polish and rehearsal.

steps.title: Create the shared deck and message the group
steps.description: Create a new Google Slides file named 'BUS101 Tesla Marketing', add 10 blank slides, and paste the link into your group chat with the message 'Deck is here, claim your slides by tomorrow.' Done when the link is sent.

steps.title: Draft the slide-by-slide skeleton
steps.description: Title the 10 slides: Title, Company overview, Target customers, Product, Pricing, Place/distribution (direct sales, no dealers), Promotion (no ads, Elon's social media, referral program), Competitor comparison, SWOT or lessons learned, Conclusion/sources. Put a name next to each slide in the group chat or deck so everyone knows their part.

steps.title: Gather sources for your slides
steps.description: Find 4-5 credible sources (Tesla investor reports, Harvard Business Review, Statista, news articles) on Tesla's 4Ps and save each link and a key fact or number into the speaker notes of your slides.

steps.title: Build your first half of the slides
steps.description: Write each of your assigned slides with a headline, 3 short bullets, and one stat or image. Done when none of your slides is blank.

steps.title: Finish remaining slides and fill gaps
steps.description: Complete your remaining slides and cover any slide a teammate hasn't started, after checking in with them in the group chat. Done when all 10 slides have real content.

steps.title: Apply a consistent design
steps.description: Pick one theme, font, and color scheme (Tesla red/black/white works), then fix alignment, shrink text walls, and add visuals such as car photos, charts, or the Supercharger map. Done when the deck looks like one person made it.

steps.title: Review the whole deck for flow and accuracy
steps.description: Read through all 10 slides in order, check that numbers match your sources, fix typos, and make sure the story flows from company to strategy to conclusion. Add a sources slide or footer citations.

steps.title: Rehearse and finalize
steps.description: Run through the presentation out loud with your group (or by yourself) once, timing it and noting transitions between speakers. Download a PDF backup and confirm everyone can open the file before bed.

grade.notes: First step has a few small decisions (naming doc, finding the prompt) and a 3-minute estimate is fine, but 'Today' vs 'Tonight' for reading Ch 3 is vague; the plan also puts ~2 hours of work in one evening with no breaks, and 'Thursday morning' may not precede a morning class deadline.

plan.taskTitle: Read Gatsby chapters 3-4 and write a 1-page response by Thursday
plan.analysis: With only today and Thursday, split reading into two timeboxed sessions with varied hooks, draft tonight, and polish Thursday morning before the deadline.

steps.title: Set up your doc and book
steps.description: Open a new doc named 'Gatsby Ch 3-4 Response', paste in the assignment prompt, and put your copy of The Great Gatsby open to chapter 3 next to your keyboard. Done when both are open and ready.

steps.title: Read Chapter 3 with a hunt
steps.description: Set a 40-minute timer and read Chapter 3 (Gatsby's party). Hook: every time you spot a rumor about who Gatsby is, jot it in your doc as a one-line bullet; done when you reach the chapter's end.

steps.title: Read Chapter 4 hunting for contradictions
steps.description: Set a 45-minute timer and read Chapter 4 (Gatsby's car ride with Nick and Jordan's story). Hook: jot down 2-3 moments where Gatsby's story doesn't add up or Nick seems unsure; done when you finish the chapter.

steps.title: Pick your angle in one sentence
steps.description: Look over your bullets and write a single sentence starting with 'In chapters 3-4, Gatsby is...' Keep the first one that feels true; done when that sentence sits at the top of your doc.

steps.title: Speed-draft the response
steps.description: Set a 30-minute timer and write about 400-500 words without stopping to edit, using your bullets and 2 short quotes from chapters 3 or 4. Challenge: don't delete anything until the timer ends; done when you have a full rough draft.

steps.title: Trim and polish to one page
steps.description: Set a 25-minute timer, read the draft aloud, fix awkward sentences, cut it down to one page, and check that your quotes are accurate. Done when it fits on one page with a title and your name.

steps.title: Submit it
steps.description: Do a last 10-minute skim for typos, then save it as a PDF or in the required format and submit or print it. Done when you've got confirmation or the page is in your bag.

grade.notes: Strong, low-pressure plan with a trivial first step, but 14 steps over 6+ months leave long gaps (Dec 9 to Jan 27) with no check-ins, so an avoider could forget. Some steps (tax-year naming, W-2s arriving by late Jan, 'Just' repeated in nearly every step) are slightly formulaic, and no step handles the dependent answer's effect on filing.

plan.taskTitle: Do my taxes (file by April 15)
plan.analysis: Spread a few small, low-pressure sessions across the months before April 15, starting with a tiny folder setup, collecting documents as they arrive in January, then filing with a comfortable buffer.

steps.title: Create one tax folder
steps.description: Just make a folder on your computer or desk named 'Taxes 2026' and drop in any tax paper or email you can spot right now. Done when the folder exists, even if it's nearly empty.

steps.title: Write a quick 'what I might need' list
steps.description: Just jot down the obvious: any jobs you had, bank accounts with interest, tuition, and any scholarships or side income. Done when you have a rough list in the folder, no perfection needed.

steps.title: Find your login info
steps.description: Just locate your logins for your school portal, bank, and employer payroll, since you'll need them to download forms later. Save the list in your folder (or a password manager) and you're done.

steps.title: Check whether someone claims you as a dependent
steps.description: Just send one short text or message to a parent or guardian asking if they'll claim you this year. Done when you've sent it and noted their answer in your folder.

steps.title: Collect your W-2s and 1099s
steps.description: Just download or photograph each form from your employers and banks as they arrive, and drop them in the folder. Done when everything on your list has a file, or you've noted which are missing.

steps.title: Download your tuition form (1098-T)
steps.description: Just log into your school portal and save the 1098-T into your folder. Done when the PDF is saved.

steps.title: Pick your filing method
steps.description: Just choose one: IRS Free File, a free student-friendly tax tool, or your campus tax help (VITA). If using VITA, put the appointment in your calendar. Done when your choice is written down.

steps.title: Create your filing account and enter basic info
steps.description: Just sign up and fill in your name, Social Security number, and address, then save and stop. Done when the account exists with your basics in it.

steps.title: Enter your income forms
steps.description: Just type in the numbers from your W-2s and 1099s, one form at a time. Done when every income form in your folder is entered.

steps.title: Enter deductions and education credits
steps.description: Just add your 1098-T info and any other credits or deductions the software asks about. Done when each section shows complete.

steps.title: Chase down anything missing
steps.description: Just contact whoever is holding up a missing form with one short email or a quick portal check. Done when you've either received it or sent the request.

steps.title: Review the return line by line
steps.description: Just read the summary and compare your numbers to your forms for typos. Done when everything matches and you've noted your refund or amount owed.

steps.title: E-file your return
steps.description: Just hit submit and save the confirmation into your folder. If you owe money, schedule the payment now. Done when you have a confirmation of acceptance.

steps.title: Save copies and celebrate
steps.description: Just download a PDF of your filed return into your folder, then do something nice for yourself. Done when the copy is saved.

grade.notes: Strong plan, but 13 steps over two weeks is slightly heavy for a ~11 hour task. Step 1 estimates 5 min but says the total is 11h5m, which doesn't add up (steps sum to ~7h). Timing is also uneven, with Step 2 landing the same day as Step 1 and a 4-day gap before Oct 5, plus the reader feedback window is tight and the 'Oct 14' submit lands on the deadline day rather than a day early as claimed.

plan.taskTitle: Write and finish my med school personal statement
plan.analysis: Start with a zero-decision setup step, then separate messy drafting from polishing across two weeks, with a short session every few days, feedback built in, and everything done a day early.

steps.title: Create the doc and paste in the prompt
steps.description: Open a new doc named 'Personal Statement - ugly draft', paste in the application's prompt and character/word limit, and type 'This is allowed to be bad' at the top. Done when the doc is saved and open; stop there.

steps.title: Dump your story moments as bullets
steps.description: Set a 30-minute timer and write messy bullet points of moments that pushed you toward medicine: clinical experiences, a person, a challenge, a turning point. Fragments are fine; stop when the timer ends, even if the list feels incomplete.

steps.title: Circle the three strongest moments
steps.description: Read your bullets and circle the three that make you feel something or that show your qualities best, going with your gut. Next to each, jot one line on what it shows about you. Done when three are circled; no more deliberating.

steps.title: Write a bullet-point skeleton
steps.description: Under the headings Opening, Why medicine, Experience 1, Experience 2, Challenge/growth, and Closing, add 2-3 bullets each from your circled moments. Bullets only, no sentences needed; stop when each heading has something under it.

steps.title: Ugly draft: opening and why medicine
steps.description: Turn the Opening and Why medicine bullets into rough paragraphs in 45 minutes. Do not edit or delete anything; if a sentence is awkward, write [fix later] and keep going.

steps.title: Ugly draft: experiences and growth
steps.description: Write rough paragraphs for Experience 1, Experience 2, and Challenge/growth from your skeleton, focusing on specific scenes and what you learned. Stop at 60 minutes even if a paragraph is unfinished.

steps.title: Ugly draft: closing and full read-through
steps.description: Write a rough closing paragraph tying back to your opening, then read the whole draft once without editing, only marking spots that feel weak. Done when the draft exists start to finish; it will be rough, and that counts as a win.

steps.title: Send the draft to one reader
steps.description: Email the draft to one trusted person, such as a pre-med advisor, professor, or mentor, asking for feedback by Oct 11. Tell them it's a rough draft and ask 'Does this sound like me, and what's unclear?' Done when sent.

steps.title: Cut to the length limit
steps.description: Without perfecting wording, trim the draft to the word or character limit by cutting repeated points and weak sentences. Done when the count fits; save as 'Draft 2'.

steps.title: Revise structure using feedback
steps.description: Read your reader's comments and make only structural changes: reorder paragraphs, strengthen the opening, clarify the 'why medicine' thread. Stop at 60 minutes and save as 'Draft 3'; leave line-level wording for the next step.

steps.title: Line-edit pass one: read aloud
steps.description: Read Draft 3 aloud and fix clunky sentences, clichés, and any [fix later] marks. Limit yourself to one pass of 45 minutes, then stop.

steps.title: Final proofread and format
steps.description: Check spelling, grammar, and the application's formatting and length rules, then save the final version as 'Personal Statement FINAL'. Stop at 30 minutes; good enough is the standard.

steps.title: Paste into the application and submit
steps.description: Paste the final statement into the application portal, check that formatting survived, and save or submit. Do not reopen the doc to tweak afterward.

grade.notes: Six steps totaling 50 min is a bit heavy for a short email reply, and the 10-min calendar step and the separate notes step add padding. 'Today' is also vague, with no time-of-day anchors to help an avoider commit.

plan.taskTitle: Reply to your professor's extension email
plan.analysis: This is a short one-sitting task, so we'll make opening the email almost effortless, then draft, check, and send it today in a few small, low-pressure steps.

steps.title: Just open the email
steps.description: Find your professor's email and open it, then leave it on screen. Done means the message is open and you've simply looked at it, nothing more.

steps.title: Jot down the key facts
steps.description: Just open a notes app and type three quick lines: what the professor asked or said, the assignment you need more time on, and the new date you'd like. Done means those three lines exist, however rough.

steps.title: Write a messy first draft
steps.description: Hit reply and just type a short, honest version: thank them, name the assignment, give a brief reason, and suggest a new date. It doesn't need to be perfect, it just needs to exist.

steps.title: Take a gentle polish pass
steps.description: Just read your draft once, fix typos, and make sure it's polite and has a clear ask and a specific new date. Done means it sounds like a respectful student, not a perfect one.

steps.title: Hit send and close the tab
steps.description: Just click send, then close the email. Done means it's in your sent folder, and you can let yourself breathe.

steps.title: Add the new date to your calendar
steps.description: Just put the date you proposed on your calendar as a tentative deadline, so you're ready whether they say yes or suggest another date.

grade.notes: Timing has issues: the 'next Thursday' deadline resolves to Oct 8, but the plan has two days with nothing scheduled (Oct 5-6 gap is fine, but Wed Oct 7 piles two steps and 'Tomorrow'/'Friday' labels mix relative and absolute dates), and total time of 4h55 is thin for a case interview with only two practice cases. Overwhelmed wording is reassuring in places ('Each step after this stands on its own'), but the later steps get bigger (45 min) without extra chunking.

plan.taskTitle: Get ready for the Deloitte behavioral + case interview
plan.analysis: We'll split prep into small daily steps: gather your stories, practice case frameworks, then rehearse out loud, finishing the day before the interview.

steps.title: Open your prep doc
steps.description: Create a doc called 'Deloitte interview prep' and paste in the job posting and your interview invite. That's it, you're done. Each step after this stands on its own.

steps.title: Highlight 5 skills in the posting
steps.description: Scan the job posting and highlight five skills or phrases that come up (like teamwork, problem solving, client focus). Paste them as a list at the top of your doc.

steps.title: List 6 past experiences
steps.description: Jot one-line bullets for six moments from classes, jobs, or clubs: a team conflict, a leadership moment, a failure, a tight deadline, and so on. Rough is fine, so just get six lines down.

steps.title: Write stories 1-3 in STAR format
steps.description: For three of your bullets, write Situation, Task, Action, Result in 2-3 short lines each. Done when each has a clear result.

steps.title: Write stories 4-6 in STAR format
steps.description: Do the same for your other three bullets. Rough notes are fine, so don't polish.

steps.title: Skim Deloitte and write 3 questions
steps.description: Read Deloitte's About page and the service line for your role. Write 3 questions to ask your interviewer and 2 facts about the firm in your doc.

steps.title: Make a case framework cheat sheet
steps.description: Read one short guide to case interviews and write a one-page cheat sheet: how to clarify, structure, analyze, and recommend. Done when it fits on a single page.

steps.title: Do practice case #1 out loud
steps.description: Find a free sample case (such as a profitability or market entry case), set a timer, and talk through it aloud using your cheat sheet. Afterwards, note two things to improve.

steps.title: Do practice case #2 and review
steps.description: Try a different type of case, aloud and timed. Check your two improvement notes from before and see if you fixed them.

steps.title: Rehearse 5 behavioral questions aloud
steps.description: Pick 5 common questions (e.g. 'Tell me about yourself,' 'a time you led a team') and answer each aloud using your STAR stories. Done when each answer is under 2 minutes.

steps.title: Set up for interview day
steps.description: Lay out your outfit, and check the time, location or video link, and who you're meeting. Put your questions for the interviewer where you can see them. Then you're ready.

grade.notes: Timing is the biggest weakness: Thursday carries 3 hours of heavy work, Friday leaves little buffer before the 5pm deadline, and 'Today' is under-used. Step 2 (gathering data) is somewhat vague, and the first step needs the rubric on hand, which can add small decisions.

plan.taskTitle: Finish Bio 201 enzyme kinetics lab report
plan.analysis: A typical lab report takes about 6 hours, so I'm spreading it across Wednesday to Friday with data and figures first, then writing, then revision before the 5pm Friday deadline.

steps.title: Set up your report document
steps.description: Create a new doc named 'Bio 201 Enzyme Kinetics Lab Report', paste in the assignment prompt and grading rubric, and drop in headings: Abstract, Introduction, Methods, Results, Discussion, References. Done when the doc is saved with all headings visible.

steps.title: Gather your raw data and lab handout
steps.description: Collect your enzyme kinetics data table, lab manual procedure, and any notes from your lab partner into one folder. Done when you can see all raw measurements (substrate concentrations and reaction rates) in one place.

steps.title: Calculate rates and build your graphs
steps.description: Calculate initial velocities, then make a Michaelis-Menten plot and a Lineweaver-Burk plot in Excel or Sheets, and estimate Km and Vmax. Done when both graphs have labeled axes with units and you have a Km and Vmax value.

steps.title: Write Methods and Results
steps.description: Describe the procedure in past tense in the Methods, then write the Results paragraphs that reference your graphs and report Km and Vmax with captioned figures and tables. Done when both sections are drafted without interpreting the numbers.

steps.title: Draft the Discussion
steps.description: Explain what your Km and Vmax mean, compare them with expected values from your textbook or lecture, and list two likely sources of error. Done when you have a rough 3-4 paragraph Discussion that answers the prompt's questions.

steps.title: Write Introduction and Abstract
steps.description: Write a short Introduction covering the enzyme, the purpose and hypothesis, and enzyme kinetics background, then write a 150-word Abstract summarizing the whole report. Done when both sections are in the doc and match your actual results.

steps.title: Add references and check against rubric
steps.description: Format your citations (lab manual, textbook, any articles) in the required style, then go through the rubric line by line and fix anything missing. Done when every rubric item is checked off.

steps.title: Proofread and submit
steps.description: Read the report aloud once, fix typos and unit errors, confirm figures are numbered and captioned, then submit it on the course site and check for the confirmation. Done when you've received the submission confirmation before 5pm.

grade.notes: Timing is the main problem: the party is on Oct 24 (the deadline), yet the invites go out Oct 5 and the cover story is set Oct 7, and the cake, food and supplies steps also land late. The first step bundles two actions, creating the doc and texting a friend, which requires deciding who to text. The boredom adaptation is mostly timers, with little real variety or gamification.

plan.taskTitle: Plan a surprise birthday party for ~15 people
plan.analysis: Lock the date and decoy plan first, then book the venue, invite guests, and handle food, decor and the cover story in varied short timeboxed sessions spaced evenly through Oct 24 with a finished buffer before the party.

steps.title: Start a party notes doc and text one co-conspirator
steps.description: Create a note titled 'Operation Surprise' and type 'Oct 24 party, ~15 people' at the top, then text one mutual friend: 'Want to help me plan a surprise party?' Done when the doc exists and the text is sent.

steps.title: Set the budget, party time and venue shortlist
steps.description: Set a 25-minute timer and fill in the doc with a total budget, a start time on Oct 24 and 3 possible venues (someone's home, a park pavilion, a party room or restaurant back room) for 15 people. Done when you have a shortlist with prices or availability noted.

steps.title: Contact venues and lock one in
steps.description: Set a 30-minute timer and call or message your top venues about Oct 24 availability, capacity and any deposit. Book the first one that fits your budget and add it to your calendar.

steps.title: Build the guest list with your co-conspirator
steps.description: Spend 20 minutes with your co-conspirator listing 15 guests with phone numbers, marking who is closest to the birthday friend and who might spill the secret. Done when the list is in the doc with contacts.

steps.title: Design and send the invite with a secrecy rule
steps.description: Make a quick invite in Canva or a text with the date, time, address and 'SHHH, it's a surprise, arrive by [time 30 minutes early]'. Send it to everyone on your list in a private group chat that excludes the birthday friend.

steps.title: Create the cover story
steps.description: Work out with your co-conspirator a believable reason to get your friend to the venue at the right time, such as a casual dinner, and who will bring them. Write the plan and a backup excuse in the doc.

steps.title: Plan the menu and drinks
steps.description: Set a 30-minute timer and decide on food for 15, such as pizza, a taco bar or catering, plus drinks and dietary needs. Write the shopping or order list with quantities and estimated cost, and place any catering order that needs notice.

steps.title: Order the cake and decorations
steps.description: Order or reserve a cake for pickup on Oct 24 and buy decorations online or list what to pick up. Challenge yourself to finish in 30 minutes, with a theme based on something your friend loves.

steps.title: Chase RSVPs and assign tasks
steps.description: Message the group chat asking for headcounts and assign small jobs: who brings ice, who helps decorate, who handles music. Done when you have a final count and each job has a name.

steps.title: Make the party playlist and a surprise moment
steps.description: Spend 30 minutes building a playlist of 2 hours or more with your friend's favorite songs. Pick a moment such as a toast, a slideshow or a group photo, and note who runs it.

steps.title: Gather photos and messages for a memory moment
steps.description: Set a 40-minute timer to collect 10 to 15 photos from the group chat and short messages from guests. Put them into a slideshow or a printed card for guests to sign.

steps.title: Confirm venue, food and cake orders
steps.description: Call or message the venue, caterer and bakery to confirm times, counts and pickup. Note any changes in the doc and settle any remaining payments.

steps.title: Buy supplies and prep a party kit
steps.description: Pick up drinks, plates, cups, candles, a lighter and tape, and pack them with the decorations in one bag or box by the door. Done when the party kit is packed.

steps.title: Send the final reminder and run-through
steps.description: Text the group the address, arrival time and the 'keep it secret' reminder, then do a 20-minute run-through with your co-conspirator of timing, who picks up the cake and who brings the birthday friend.

grade.notes: Sequencing and timing have flaws: photographing rooms (Oct 22) happens after packing is mostly done, so it doesn't capture the original condition, and the final walkthrough/cleaning is thin (bedroom, living room, and the move itself are squeezed in with no final-day buffer). Pacing is also unrealistic for the total time (18h40 estimate vs. the listed step times, which sum to roughly 15h) and gaps exist in the early plan (donation drop-off, packing supplies before 'pack stuff'), plus 'Do the steps' overwhelm reassurance is only present in a few steps.

plan.taskTitle: Move out of my apartment by end of October
plan.analysis: Moving out is a big multi-week job, so it's split into many tiny, standalone steps paced evenly through October, with bookings and notices first, packing by room, then cleaning and key return, finishing a day early.

steps.title: Put 5 empty boxes or bags by the door
steps.description: Grab any boxes, bags or laundry baskets you already have and set them by your front door. That's it, you're done, and this step stands on its own.

steps.title: Find your lease and read the move-out section
steps.description: Open your lease and locate the notice requirement, move-out date, and cleaning rules. Write the notice deadline and move-out date on a sticky note or in your notes app.

steps.title: Send your move-out notice
steps.description: Email your landlord or property manager confirming your move-out date and ask about the walkthrough and key return. Done when the email is sent.

steps.title: Decide how you're moving and book it
steps.description: Pick one option (friend with a car, rental van, or movers) and send one message or booking request for your move date. Done when it's requested or confirmed.

steps.title: Make a list of utilities and accounts to update
steps.description: List internet, electricity, renters insurance, and mail, then note which ones need a stop or transfer date. Just the list for now.

steps.title: Schedule utility shutoffs and address changes
steps.description: Using your list, call or fill in forms to set end dates for internet and electricity. Do as many as you can; the rest can wait for the next step.

steps.title: Order or collect more packing supplies
steps.description: Get tape, markers, and enough boxes from a store, a friend, or an online order. Done when you have supplies arriving or in hand.

steps.title: Pack the stuff you never use
steps.description: Box up off-season clothes, books, decor and anything on high shelves. Stop after 45 minutes, even if it's not finished.

steps.title: Sort the closet into keep, donate, trash
steps.description: Pull everything out of one closet and make three piles. Bag the donate pile and put it by the door.

steps.title: Drop off donations
steps.description: Take the donate bags to a donation center or drop-off bin. Done when your hands are empty.

steps.title: Pack the bedroom
steps.description: Pack everything in the bedroom except what you need for the next two weeks. Label each box with the room name.

steps.title: Pack the living room
steps.description: Box up decor, media, cables and anything non-essential in the living room. Label each box.

steps.title: Pack the bathroom extras
steps.description: Pack spare toiletries, towels and cleaning supplies you won't use this week. Leave only daily basics out.

steps.title: Pack the kitchen, part one
steps.description: Pack rarely used dishes, small appliances and pantry items you won't eat. Label the boxes.

steps.title: Photograph every room
steps.description: Take quick photos of each room, walls, floors and appliances, to document the apartment's condition. Save them in one album.

steps.title: Pack the kitchen, part two
steps.description: Pack the remaining dishes and cookware, keeping only one plate, one bowl, one mug and one pan. Done when the cabinets are mostly empty.

steps.title: Do a stragglers sweep and confirm moving help
steps.description: Walk each room for leftover items and drop them into a box. Then text your helper or mover to confirm the time.

steps.title: Clean the kitchen
steps.description: Wipe cabinets, counters, stove and sink, and clean out the fridge. Done when surfaces are clear and wiped.

steps.title: Clean the bathroom
steps.description: Scrub the toilet, sink, and shower, and wipe the mirror. Done when it looks ready for the walkthrough.

steps.title: Move day: load and haul
steps.description: Load your boxes and furniture and take everything to your new place. Take it one trip at a time; you just need to get it out.

steps.title: Sweep and vacuum the empty rooms
steps.description: Sweep and vacuum every room, and take out the last trash. Done when floors are clear.

steps.title: Final walkthrough and return keys
steps.description: Check each room against your photos, close the windows, and hand in your keys as your landlord asked. Done when keys are returned and you have confirmation by text or email.

grade.notes: The total is only about 16 hours, but the step list sums to roughly 12 hours, so the stated total doesn't match. Step 15 hides a booking inside a session, and the 'Free trial' tutor sessions #2 and #3 aren't free. Sessions are spaced every 3-4 days at 30 minutes, which is too light to reach real conversational ability in 11 weeks. The step count is big, but each step is small.

plan.taskTitle: Learn survival Spanish for your Mexico trip
plan.analysis: Build a realistic ~16-hour survival-Spanish habit over 11 weeks with short, varied sessions (apps, audio, speaking, real-life scenarios) that rotate topics, with a final dress rehearsal before Dec 20.

steps.title: Install a Spanish app and put it on your home screen
steps.description: Download Duolingo (or Babbel) and put it on your phone's home screen, then open a note titled 'Mexico Spanish' to keep phrases in. Done when both are ready and you've tapped through the first lesson screen.

steps.title: Greetings and politeness sprint
steps.description: Set a 25-minute timer and learn hola, buenos días, por favor, gracias, perdón, con permiso, and cómo está. Done when you can say all seven out loud without looking, and have saved them to your note.

steps.title: Numbers 1-100 and prices challenge
steps.description: Spend 30 minutes learning numbers and how to ask '¿Cuánto cuesta?'. Challenge: read 10 random prices from a grocery site aloud in Spanish with no peeking.

steps.title: Food and ordering drill
steps.description: Set a 30-minute timer and learn 25 menu words (agua, pollo, sin, la cuenta, etc.) plus 'Quisiera...' and 'Me gustaría...'. Done when you can order a full meal aloud from a Mexican restaurant menu online.

steps.title: Listen to a beginner Spanish podcast episode
steps.description: Take a walk with Coffee Break Spanish (Season 1) or similar and play one episode. Jot down 5 new phrases in your note when you get back.

steps.title: Directions and transport lesson
steps.description: Learn dónde está, a la derecha, a la izquierda, derecho, el baño, la estación, el taxi, el aeropuerto. Done when you've answered 10 flashcards on a free deck (Anki or Quizlet) correctly.

steps.title: Record yourself in a mock taxi conversation
steps.description: Write a 6-line dialogue asking a driver to take you to a hotel and how much it costs, then record yourself saying it on your phone. Done when you've played it back and re-recorded once to fix one mistake.

steps.title: Book a free conversation session
steps.description: Schedule a 30-minute trial on italki or Preply, or a Spanish conversation meetup, and add it to your calendar for late October. Done when the booking is confirmed.

steps.title: Review week: flashcards and weak spots
steps.description: Run 30 minutes of mixed flashcards on everything so far and star the 10 phrases you miss most. Done when you've gotten those 10 right twice in a row.

steps.title: Conversation session #1
steps.description: Attend your booked session and tell your tutor you're preparing for Mexico. Practice greetings, ordering, and directions, and note 3 corrections afterward.

steps.title: Hotel and lodging phrases
steps.description: Spend 30 minutes on 'Tengo una reservación', 'Una habitación para dos', wifi, key, checkout time, and 'Necesito ayuda'. Done when you've role-played check-in out loud twice.

steps.title: Shopping and bargaining at the market
steps.description: Learn 'Me lo llevo', 'Es muy caro', '¿Tiene algo más barato?', sizes and colors. Challenge: haggle aloud over three imaginary souvenirs.

steps.title: Watch a Spanish YouTube video with subtitles
steps.description: Watch a 15-minute Mexico travel vlog in Spanish with Spanish subtitles and count how many words you recognize. Write down 8 new words and add them to your deck.

steps.title: Emergency and health phrases
steps.description: Learn 'Necesito un médico', 'Me duele...', farmacia, policía, 'Estoy perdido/a', 'No entiendo', and 'Más despacio, por favor'. Done when you can say each one from memory and have saved them to your phone's favorites note.

steps.title: Conversation session #2
steps.description: Book and do another 30-minute tutoring session focused on role-playing restaurants, directions, and a problem at the hotel. Ask the tutor to speak at normal speed.

steps.title: Learn essential verbs and sentence patterns
steps.description: Spend 45 minutes on quiero, necesito, puedo, tengo, voy, estoy, and 'Me gustaría'. Build 12 original sentences for your trip and say each aloud.

steps.title: Mexican Spanish slang and culture check
steps.description: Read a short guide to Mexican Spanish (mande, ahorita, qué padre, propina etiquette). Add 8 items to your note and quiz yourself once.

steps.title: Mock full-trip role play
steps.description: Set a 40-minute timer and run through airport, taxi, hotel, restaurant, and market scenes out loud, recording yourself. Done when you've listened back and marked 5 weak spots.

steps.title: Drill your 5 weak spots
steps.description: Spend 30 minutes making flashcards and sentences for the weak spots from your mock role play. Done when you've nailed each three times in a row.

steps.title: Conversation session #3
steps.description: Do a 45-minute tutoring session simulating a complete day in Mexico City, and ask for feedback on your pronunciation of numbers and food words.

steps.title: Download offline tools
steps.description: Download Google Translate's Spanish offline pack and Spanish maps for your destination, and screenshot your key phrases note. Done when you've tested it in airplane mode.

steps.title: Listening practice with native speed audio
steps.description: Listen to a 30-minute Mexican Spanish podcast or radio clip (e.g. Radio Ambulante or a Mexican news segment). Challenge: catch and note 10 words you know.

steps.title: Mock full-trip role play, round two
steps.description: Repeat your five scenes from memory with no notes, recording yourself. Done when you finish all scenes with fewer mistakes than in November.

steps.title: Final flashcard review and cheat sheet
steps.description: Spend 30 minutes reviewing your full deck, then save a one-page cheat sheet of your top 40 phrases to your phone and print a copy. Done when the cheat sheet is in your bag or luggage list.

grade.notes: The first step bundles opening the file, writing a 4-node test, running it and recording results, which is more than 5 minutes and requires some decisions. Timing is vague, with only 'Today' and 'Tonight' and no clock times, and the 'submit 30 min early' buffer is not built into the schedule.

plan.taskTitle: Fix linked list delete bug in CS 106 assignment
plan.analysis: Since the deadline is tonight, compress into one focused evening: set up a reproducible failing case, trace the delete logic on paper, fix it, then test and submit with buffer.

steps.title: Open the project and write a failing delete test
steps.description: Open your linked list file and add a tiny test in main that builds a 4-node list, deletes the second node, and prints the list. Run it once and write down what you see versus what you expected; done when you've seen the bug happen.

steps.title: Add print statements around delete
steps.description: Print the node being deleted, its previous node, and its next node before and after the pointer changes inside your delete function. Rerun your test and note exactly where the chain breaks.

steps.title: Trace delete on paper for each case
steps.description: Draw boxes and arrows and walk through your delete code line by line for deleting the head, a middle node, and the tail. Mark the line where a pointer gets overwritten or skipped, such as relinking prev->next after you've already moved the pointer.

steps.title: Fix the pointer logic
steps.description: Rewrite the faulty lines so prev->next is set to the deleted node's next before freeing it, and handle the head and empty-list cases separately. Done when your 4-node test prints the three remaining nodes correctly.

steps.title: Test edge cases
steps.description: Run deletes on the head, the tail, the only node, a value not in the list, and two deletes in a row. Fix anything that fails and remove your debugging prints.

steps.title: Check for leaks and submit
steps.description: If your course uses Valgrind or similar, run it to confirm no leaks or invalid frees, then reread the assignment spec for submission requirements. Submit at least 30 minutes before 11:59pm.

grade.notes: Seven steps and about 3 hours is a bit heavy for a 500-word discussion post, and the polish steps risk feeding perfectionism. The timing also leaves Sunday as the deadline day for both polishing and posting, and the plan claims 'finishing a day early' when it doesn't.

plan.taskTitle: Write a 500-word Psych 101 discussion post on the bystander effect
plan.analysis: Start with a tiny setup step, then separate rough drafting from polishing across a few short sessions spread through the week, finishing a day early.

steps.title: Open a doc and paste in the prompt
steps.description: Create a new doc named 'Psych 101 bystander post' and paste in the discussion prompt and any rubric or word limit. Done when the doc is open with the prompt at the top; do nothing else.

steps.title: Skim your textbook section on the bystander effect
steps.description: Read the bystander effect section in your Psych 101 textbook or lecture notes, and copy 3-5 key points into the doc as bullets, including Kitty Genovese, Darley and Latané, and diffusion of responsibility. Bullet fragments are fine; stop after 30 minutes even if you feel unfinished.

steps.title: Write a messy bullet skeleton
steps.description: Under your notes, type 4 bullets: your hook, what the bystander effect is, one study or real example, and your own take or a way to reduce it. Bullet points are fine and nothing needs to be good; stop once all 4 bullets have something in them.

steps.title: Write an ugly first draft
steps.description: Turn each bullet into a few sentences without editing, deleting or checking word count until the end. The goal is a rough draft of about 500 words, and it is supposed to be bad; stop when you reach the end of your last bullet or hit 45 minutes.

steps.title: Take a break, then do one structural pass
steps.description: Reread the draft once and only fix big things: move a paragraph, cut or add to reach roughly 450-550 words, and make sure you answer the prompt. Do not fix wording yet; stop after 30 minutes.

steps.title: Polish and add citations
steps.description: Fix typos and awkward sentences, read it aloud once, and add your textbook citation or any source your prompt requires. Good enough is the standard; stop after 40 minutes.

steps.title: Post it and check the submission
steps.description: Copy the post into the discussion board, submit it, and confirm it shows up. Done means it is posted, with no more edits afterward.

grade.notes: Strong low-pressure, tiny first step, but the 12 steps and 5-hour total is a bit heavy; analysis says three weeks while the plan ends Oct 16, and step 12's 'three visits in a row of weeks' wording is garbled. Also 'Today' step 1 then no step covering the first-visit anxiety (what to do if gym feels intimidating) or a fallback if a session is missed.

plan.taskTitle: Ease into a regular gym habit
plan.analysis: With no deadline, we'll spread tiny, low-pressure steps over about three weeks, starting with setup and a short visit, then building to a repeatable weekly routine.

steps.title: Put your gym clothes by the door
steps.description: Just grab a t-shirt, shorts or leggings, socks, and sneakers and set them in a pile by your door or in your bag. Done when you can see them without opening anything.

steps.title: Find out where the gym is and when it's open
steps.description: Just look up your campus rec center or nearest gym, and put its hours and walking route into your phone's notes or maps. Done when you know the open hours and the address.

steps.title: Take a gentle first visit
steps.description: Just walk in, look around, and do 15 minutes of easy walking on a treadmill or bike. Leaving after that counts as a full win.

steps.title: Put three gym slots in your calendar
steps.description: Just pick three days next week, such as Monday, Wednesday, and Friday, and add 40-minute blocks to your calendar. Done when all three show up.

steps.title: Write a tiny starter routine
steps.description: Just jot down 4 easy exercises, like a treadmill warm-up, leg press, rows, and a plank, with 2 sets each. Keep it to one note you can follow without thinking.

steps.title: Do your first routine session
steps.description: Just follow your note for 40 minutes, keeping the weights light. Done when you've finished the list, even slowly.

steps.title: Do your second session
steps.description: Just repeat your routine, and add one more set to a single exercise if it feels okay. Done when you've checked it off in your calendar.

steps.title: Do your third session
steps.description: Just go and repeat the routine again, and notice what feels easier than before. Done when you've finished and jotted one line about how it went.

steps.title: Tweak your routine and book next week
steps.description: Just swap out any exercise you disliked, and add three new calendar blocks for the following week. Done when next week's sessions are scheduled.

steps.title: Week two, session one
steps.description: Just show up for your tweaked routine for about 45 minutes. Done when you've completed it.

steps.title: Week two, session two
steps.description: Just go again and do your routine, with a little extra time on whichever exercise you liked best. Done when it's finished and checked off.

steps.title: Week two, session three
steps.description: Just go for your third visit of the week and finish your routine. Done when you've hit three visits in a row of weeks, which is a real habit starting.

grade.notes: Study volume is far too light for a 6-week LSAT push (about 9 hours total, with only one or two sessions per week and gaps of up to 9 days), and the plan never covers Logic Games-free but essential full-length practice tests. The overwhelmed style is handled well with small, bounded steps, but there is little explicit reassurance and the schedule is thin.

plan.taskTitle: Study for the LSAT (test day Nov 14)
plan.analysis: Start with a tiny setup step, take a baseline section, then alternate short drills and timed practice on Logical Reasoning and Reading Comprehension, finishing the day before the test.

steps.title: Make your LSAT note and calendar entry
steps.description: Open a new note titled 'LSAT plan' and type 'Test: Nov 14' at the top. Then add 'LSAT' to your calendar on Nov 14. That's all, and this step stands on its own.

steps.title: Set up free LawHub practice
steps.description: Create a free LSAC LawHub account and bookmark the page with the free PrepTests. You don't need to pick a test or start one yet.

steps.title: Take one timed Logical Reasoning section
steps.description: Open one PrepTest and do a single 35-minute Logical Reasoning section. Your score doesn't matter, you're just seeing where you start.

steps.title: Log your misses
steps.description: Go through the questions you missed and write each one in your note with its type, such as flaw, assumption, or strengthen. Done means you have a list, not a fix.

steps.title: Drill Logical Reasoning flaw and assumption questions
steps.description: Do 10 flaw or assumption questions untimed and read each explanation. Done means you've written one sentence about the pattern you noticed.

steps.title: Try two Reading Comprehension passages
steps.description: Do two RC passages untimed and jot a one-line main point for each before answering. Then check your answers.

steps.title: Timed Reading Comprehension section plus review
steps.description: Do one 35-minute RC section, then spend 25 minutes reviewing every miss. Add the misses to your note.

steps.title: Drill your weakest Logical Reasoning type
steps.description: Look at your miss list, pick the most common type, and do 10 more questions of that type. Done means you've reviewed each wrong answer.

steps.title: Review RC passages with attention to structure
steps.description: Do two more RC passages and mark the author's main point and tone in each paragraph. Check your answers when you finish.

steps.title: Timed Logical Reasoning section plus review
steps.description: Take one 35-minute LR section from a new PrepTest, then spend 25 minutes reviewing your misses. Compare to your first section from Oct 3.

steps.title: Timed RC section plus review
steps.description: Do one new 35-minute RC section, then review each miss for 25 minutes. Update your miss log.

steps.title: Two-section timed practice
steps.description: Do one LR and one RC section back to back with a short break, then glance at your score. Note only one thing to focus on next.

steps.title: Review your miss log
steps.description: Reread your note and redo 5 questions you missed before. Stop there, since no new material is needed.

steps.title: Set up for test day
steps.description: Check your test time and location or login details, and put your ID and anything else you need where you'll see it. Then you're done studying.

grade.notes: Strong perfectionist framing with ugly-draft permission and stop rules, but the 22-hour total looks light for 25 pages with a real literature search, and there is no step for finding missing sources. Step 2 (45 min, 'every source') is a bit large for a first-day action after the tiny step 1, and the plan has no buffer or catch-up time before Oct 30.

plan.taskTitle: Write thesis Chapter 2: literature review (~25 pages)
plan.analysis: Start with a tiny setup action, then pace roughly 22 hours of work across the month in short sessions: gather and map sources, write ugly first drafts section by section, then separate revision passes, finishing a few days before Oct 31.

steps.title: Create the Chapter 2 file
steps.description: Open a new doc named 'Ch2 Lit Review - UGLY DRAFT', type the title 'Chapter 2: Literature Review' at the top, and save it in your thesis folder. Done when the file exists; stop there.

steps.title: Dump every source into one list
steps.description: Paste every paper, book and note you already have for the thesis into a messy list at the bottom of the doc, with no sorting and no reading. Done when the list is pasted or after 45 minutes, whichever comes first.

steps.title: Cluster sources into themes
steps.description: Group your sources under 4-6 rough theme headings tied to your research question, and bullet points and typos are fine. Done when every source sits under a heading, even if some are labeled 'Unsure'.

steps.title: Sketch a bullet-point skeleton
steps.description: Turn your theme headings into section headings with 2-3 bullets each saying what that section will argue, plus a rough page target totaling about 25 pages. Done when the outline fits on one page; it does not need to be good.

steps.title: Read and annotate key sources, theme 1
steps.description: Skim the 4-5 most central sources for your first theme and write 2-3 sentence notes on each: claim, method, and how it relates to your question. Stop after 90 minutes even if you are not done.

steps.title: Read and annotate key sources, theme 2
steps.description: Do the same quick skim-and-note pass for the second theme's key sources, with rough notes only. Stop when the timer ends.

steps.title: Read and annotate key sources, themes 3-4
steps.description: Skim and note the key sources for your remaining themes, making a short note per source. Stop after 2 hours; unfinished sources can wait.

steps.title: Ugly draft: introduction and theme 1
steps.description: Write the chapter intro (half a page) and the first theme section as fast and badly as you like, using [CITE] placeholders if you cannot find a reference. Stop after 2 hours or when the section has a rough start-to-end, whichever comes first.

steps.title: Ugly draft: theme 2
steps.description: Write the second section without editing or rereading, and leave bullet points wherever sentences will not come. Done when the section reaches its rough page target or at the 2-hour mark.

steps.title: Ugly draft: theme 3
steps.description: Write the third section in the same fast, messy style, with no polishing allowed. Stop at 2 hours.

steps.title: Ugly draft: theme 4 and any remaining themes
steps.description: Draft the remaining theme sections quickly, bullets allowed. Stop at 2 hours; this is a draft, not the final text.

steps.title: Ugly draft: gaps and conclusion
steps.description: Write a rough section naming the gaps in the literature that your thesis fills, then a half-page summary. Done when the whole chapter exists from intro to end, however rough.

steps.title: Structure pass only
steps.description: Read the draft once for flow only: reorder sections, add a one-sentence topic signpost to each section, and cut obvious repetition. Do not fix wording yet; stop after 1 hour 30 minutes.

steps.title: Fill citations and placeholders
steps.description: Search your doc for every [CITE] and bullet placeholder and replace each with a proper reference or sentence. Done when none remain, or after 2 hours, with leftovers listed.

steps.title: Polish pass and reference list
steps.description: Fix wording and formatting section by section and make the reference list consistent with your department's style. Stop at 2 hours; good enough is the goal, not perfect.

steps.title: Final read-through and send
steps.description: Read the chapter once start to finish, fix only typos and clear errors, and then send or file it with your supervisor. Done when it is submitted, with no more rewriting.

grade.notes: The resolved due date of 2026-10-04 is a Sunday, and 'this week' could end Friday (Oct 2), so the buffer is unclear. Step 4 depends on the call actually reaching someone, which a voicemail outcome breaks. Steps 2 and 3 could be done together today, and the plan uses 'Just' a lot, which is only moderately low-pressure.

plan.taskTitle: Call the dentist to book a cleaning
plan.analysis: This is a quick one-sitting chore, so a tiny first step, a short call, and a calendar entry get it done by the end of the week.

steps.title: Put the dentist's number on your screen
steps.description: Just find the dentist's phone number and type or save it in your phone's notes or contacts so it's ready to tap. Done when the number is sitting on your screen, no calling yet.

steps.title: Jot down 2-3 times that work
steps.description: Just glance at your calendar and write down two or three days or times this week or next that could work for a cleaning. Any would-be options are fine, and nothing has to be perfect.

steps.title: Make the quick call
steps.description: Just tap the number and say, "Hi, I'd like to schedule a cleaning." If they don't answer, leave a short voicemail with your name and number, and that still counts as done.

steps.title: Add the appointment to your calendar
steps.description: Just put the date and time they gave you into your calendar, plus any note about arrival time or forms. Done when it shows up on your calendar.

grade.notes: The first step is tiny and concrete, but some sequencing is off: the LinkedIn work in steps 6 and 7 comes before the resume is finalized in step 8, so LinkedIn may need re-editing after the reviewer feedback. The feedback step is sent Saturday with only a Monday turnaround, so the reviewer may not reply in time. The claim of finishing a day before the fair is accurate, but Tuesday's printing step is fairly heavy and leaves no buffer.

plan.taskTitle: Update resume and LinkedIn before the career fair
plan.analysis: Update the resume first as the source of truth, get quick feedback, then mirror it on LinkedIn in short sessions spread across the week, finishing a day before the fair.

steps.title: Open your resume and make a working copy
steps.description: Find your current resume file, duplicate it, and name the copy 'Resume_2026_Fall'. Open LinkedIn in another tab. Done when both are open side by side.

steps.title: Add new experiences to a running list
steps.description: At the top of your new resume copy, jot down every job, class project, club role, or award since your last update, with rough dates. Done when nothing recent is missing, even if it's messy.

steps.title: Rewrite experience bullets
steps.description: For each role and project, write 2-4 bullets starting with an action verb and including a number or result where you can (e.g. 'Organized event for 60 members'). Done when every entry has polished bullets.

steps.title: Update education, skills, and formatting
steps.description: Add your current GPA if strong, relevant coursework, and updated skills and tools. Fix fonts, spacing, and alignment so it fits one page. Done when it looks clean as a single page.

steps.title: Get feedback on your resume
steps.description: Email the PDF to a friend or visit your campus career center (or use their online resume review) and ask for specific feedback on clarity and typos. Done when the request is sent or appointment booked.

steps.title: Rewrite your LinkedIn headline and About section
steps.description: Write a headline with your major, year, and target field, then a 3-4 sentence About section using your resume's strongest points. Done when both are saved on your profile.

steps.title: Update LinkedIn experience, skills, and photo
steps.description: Copy your new resume bullets into each LinkedIn entry, add new skills, and check that your profile photo is clear and professional. Done when your profile matches your resume.

steps.title: Apply feedback and finalize resume
steps.description: Make the edits from your reviewer, proofread out loud once, and export the final PDF with a clear file name. Done when the final PDF is saved.

steps.title: Print copies and prep for the fair
steps.description: Print 8-10 copies of your resume on good paper, put them in a folder, and add the fair's list of employers you want to visit. Also add your LinkedIn URL or QR code to the resume if missing. Done when your folder is by your bag.

grade.notes: First step is 5 min but requires writing or pasting 36 cards, which is more than a tiny start and involves a small decision (index cards vs app). Some mismatches: step 3 and 4 say 30 min but the described work totals less, and the song/game variety promised in the analysis is only lightly delivered after Saturday.

plan.taskTitle: Memorize the first 36 elements (H to Kr) for Monday's chem quiz
plan.analysis: Split the 36 elements into chunks of 9, vary the method each session (flashcards, mnemonics, songs, blank-table recall, games), and space out reviews so everything sticks by Monday.

steps.title: Set up your element study kit
steps.description: Grab 36 index cards or open a blank flashcard app deck, and write or paste in H through Kr in order, with the symbol on one side and the name on the other. Done when the deck sits on your desk or screen ready to use.

steps.title: Learn elements 1-9 (H to F) with a 20-minute timer
steps.description: Set a 20-minute timer and go through H, He, Li, Be, B, C, N, O, F, saying each name and symbol aloud and inventing a silly image for each. Done when you can run all 9 cards without a mistake.

steps.title: Learn elements 10-18 (Ne to Ar)
steps.description: Do a 5-minute quick review of 1-9, then learn Ne, Na, Mg, Al, Si, P, S, Cl, Ar using a mnemonic or the Na = sodium/natrium style of oddball hook. Done when all 18 cards run clean.

steps.title: Learn elements 19-27 (K to Co)
steps.description: Set a 20-minute timer and learn K, Ca, Sc, Ti, V, Cr, Mn, Fe, Co. Pay extra attention to the symbols that don't match the name, like K and Fe. Done when you can recite them in order, then review 1-18 for 5 minutes.

steps.title: Sing it: elements 28-36 plus a song run
steps.description: Learn Ni, Cu, Zn, Ga, Ge, As, Se, Br, Kr, then play the Tom Lehrer or AsapSCIENCE periodic table song and sing along through element 36. Challenge: finish the song without peeking at your cards.

steps.title: Blank-table recall challenge
steps.description: Write elements 1-36 from memory on a blank sheet with a 10-minute timer, then check against your deck and circle every miss. Done when you have a short list of your weakest elements to target.

steps.title: Drill your weak spots and play a shuffled round
steps.description: Spend 15 minutes on the circled elements with new mnemonics, then shuffle the deck and go through all 36 in random order, beating your last score. Done when you get 34+ of 36 right.

steps.title: Final quick-fire check
steps.description: Do one last blank-table write-out of H to Kr in 10 minutes, and fix any remaining slips. Done when it's perfect or nearly, then stop and rest before the quiz.

grade.notes: Step 1 is tiny, but pasting the resume as well as the job posting adds a small extra task, and the plan puts the polish and submission on the deadline day with no buffer. If anything slips on Friday, the application is late, and the plan never says to ask for feedback or include a reserve block.

plan.taskTitle: Write and submit the Google APM cover letter
plan.analysis: Split the work into a tiny setup step, an ugly-draft phase, and a separate capped polish phase, spread across Wednesday to Friday so nothing is rushed or perfected.

steps.title: Open the doc and paste in the job posting
steps.description: Create a new doc named 'Google APM cover letter', paste in the APM job description and your current resume below it. Done when both are pasted; do not read or edit anything yet.

steps.title: Dump rough bullet notes on 3 stories
steps.description: Under the heading 'Ugly notes', write messy bullets for why Google, why product management, and 2 projects where you led, built or solved a problem for users. Bullet fragments are fine and nobody will see this; stop after 30 minutes even if it feels incomplete.

steps.title: Write an ugly first draft of the opening and body
steps.description: Turn your bullets into paragraphs: a 3-sentence opening, then one paragraph per story. It is supposed to be bad; do not edit as you go, and stop at 45 minutes or when you have 3 paragraphs, whichever comes first.

steps.title: Write the closing and finish the full rough draft
steps.description: Add a short closing paragraph saying why you're excited and asking for a conversation, then read the draft top to bottom once without changing anything. Done when the draft has a beginning, middle and end, however rough.

steps.title: Polish pass 1: content only
steps.description: Compare the draft to the job description and tweak each story to match one or two Google APM qualities, cutting anything vague. Allow yourself one pass only and stop at 40 minutes; sentence-level wording waits for the next step.

steps.title: Polish pass 2: tighten, proofread, submit
steps.description: Trim to one page, fix typos by reading it aloud once, save as a PDF named with your name, and attach it to the application. Stop at 25 minutes, then submit; good enough is the finish line.

grade.notes: Steps 2-6 are copy-paste generic ('class 1...class 5') and never name the real classes or ask the student to pick an order, and the 40-minute per-class blocks are not broken into smaller pieces for an overwhelmed student. Step 1 also involves some gathering and labeling that isn't strictly 5 minutes; the timeline stays inside the deadline but leaves Oct 8-9 unused with no buffer mention.

plan.taskTitle: Organize notes for all 5 classes before midterms
plan.analysis: We'll split this into one small session per class, spread across the week, so each step stands on its own and you can't get overwhelmed.

steps.title: Gather everything and make 5 folders
steps.description: Pile every notebook, loose page and laptop note file in one spot. Create 5 empty folders or dividers, one per class, and label them. That's all for today, and you're done.

steps.title: Organize class 1 notes
steps.description: Put the pages or files for your first class in date order and drop them in its folder. Write a one-line list of the topics covered. Done when the folder is in order, even if the notes are messy.

steps.title: Organize class 2 notes
steps.description: Same as before, for your second class: date order, into its folder, a one-line topic list. This step doesn't depend on how yesterday went.

steps.title: Organize class 3 notes
steps.description: Sort the third class's notes by date, file them, and jot a topic list. Stop when the folder is done.

steps.title: Organize class 4 notes
steps.description: Sort the fourth class's notes by date, file them, and write the topic list. A short, easy session.

steps.title: Organize class 5 notes
steps.description: Sort your last class's notes by date, file them, and write the topic list. After this, all 5 classes are organized.

steps.title: List missing notes and ask for them
steps.description: Look over your 5 topic lists and write down any lectures with gaps. Message a classmate or check the course site for those notes. Done when you've sent the requests.

steps.title: Make a one-page study map
steps.description: Combine your 5 topic lists on one page, with each class's midterm date at the top. Slot in any notes you got back. Done when you have one page you can start studying from.

grade.notes: Strong, concrete plan with a tiny first step, but 14 steps may be a lot for a group project, and step 9 (revise using teammate feedback) has no earlier step where teammates actually leave comments. Step 4 is also placed on Oct 5 after a Friday kickoff with no gap, and the Oct 19 submission leaves just one day of buffer.

plan.taskTitle: Build a marketing plan for a local coffee shop with your 3 teammates
plan.analysis: Start by getting the team in one place with a shared doc, then spread research, strategy, drafting, and review sessions evenly across three weeks so the plan is finished a day before Oct 20.

steps.title: Create the shared doc and message the team
steps.description: Create a Google Doc titled 'Coffee Shop Marketing Plan', paste in the assignment prompt, and send the link to your 3 teammates with the message 'Can everyone add their available times this week?'. Done when the message is sent.

steps.title: Hold the kickoff meeting and split roles
steps.description: Meet for 45 minutes to confirm which coffee shop you're using, then assign each person a section: market and competitors, target customers, strategy and channels, budget and timeline. Write names next to each section in the doc.

steps.title: Visit the coffee shop and note what you see
steps.description: Go to the shop (or its social pages and website if you can't visit) and write down 10 observations: menu and prices, busy times, décor, customers, and what social accounts they post on. Add them under a 'Shop Observations' heading in the doc.

steps.title: Research your assigned section
steps.description: Spend one session gathering facts for your section, such as 3 nearby competitors, local demographics, or typical café marketing costs. Done when you have a bulleted list of at least 6 sourced facts in the doc.

steps.title: Draft your assigned section
steps.description: Turn your research bullets into a first draft of about 1 page for your section, with a clear recommendation or finding. It's fine if it's rough as long as it's written in the doc.

steps.title: Hold the midpoint check-in
steps.description: Meet for 30 minutes to read each other's drafts and agree on one target customer and 3 main marketing goals. Write the agreed goals at the top of the doc.

steps.title: Develop campaign ideas and channels
steps.description: Using the agreed goals, write 3 specific campaign ideas (for example a loyalty card, a local student discount, or an Instagram series), each with its channel, cost, and expected result. Add them to your section.

steps.title: Build the budget and 3-month timeline
