steps.description: Whoever owns budget and timeline creates a table with each campaign's costs and launch dates, while the others send their cost estimates. Done when the table is in the doc and totals add up.

steps.title: Revise your section using teammate feedback
steps.description: Read the comments teammates left on your section and fix the 5 most important issues. Resolve each comment when it's addressed.

steps.title: Assemble the full plan and write the intro and summary
steps.description: Combine all sections in one order, write a half-page executive summary, and make formatting and fonts consistent. Done when the doc reads top to bottom as one plan.

steps.title: Make the presentation or deliverable materials
steps.description: If a presentation is required, create about 8 slides with one for each section and split speaking parts. Otherwise make a one-page visual summary of the campaigns and timeline.

steps.title: Proofread the full plan
steps.description: Read the whole document out loud, fixing typos and unclear sentences and checking that numbers match between the budget and the text. Done when you've been through every page once.

steps.title: Hold the final team review and rehearsal
steps.description: Meet for an hour to go over the final plan, practice presenting if needed, and confirm who will submit it. Fix any last problems that come up.

steps.title: Submit the finished plan
steps.description: Export to PDF or upload the final files, double-check that all 4 names are on it, and submit it. Done when you see the submission confirmation.

grade.notes: Step 2 reads 20 minutes before the page count is known, and the 8-session divisor is fixed before checking remaining pages. The schedule has gaps and inconsistencies: Session 4 is only 30 min but must cover the full page target, and 45-minute sessions may not finish the book, so the plan may not complete it.

plan.taskTitle: Finish reading Sapiens
plan.analysis: With no deadline, spread the remaining reading over about two weeks in short timeboxed sessions that vary the format and include small hooks so it never gets dull.

steps.title: Set up your reading spot
steps.description: Put your copy of Sapiens on your pillow or desk, and place a pen and a sticky note on top. Done when the book is open to where you stopped and a bookmark marks the spot.

steps.title: Read 20 minutes with a timer
steps.description: Set a 20-minute timer and read from your bookmark without stopping. When it rings, jot one surprising fact on the sticky note.

steps.title: Count your remaining pages
steps.description: Check how many pages are left and divide by 8 sessions to get your per-session page target. Write that number on the sticky note and keep it in the book.

steps.title: Session 1: 45 minutes of reading
steps.description: Set a 45-minute timer and read your target pages. Challenge: finish a chapter before the timer ends, then write one sentence on what it argued.

steps.title: Session 2: Read somewhere new
steps.description: Take the book to a cafe, library, or park bench and read for 45 minutes. Change of scenery is your hook; stop when the timer ends and note a favorite quote.

steps.title: Session 3: Read and mark ideas
steps.description: Read for 45 minutes with a pen in hand, underlining the single boldest claim in each chapter section. Done when you have at least 3 underlines.

steps.title: Session 4: Audiobook or sample swap
steps.description: Spend 30 minutes switching format: listen to the matching chapter of the Sapiens audiobook while walking or doing chores, or read aloud for 10 pages. Done when you have covered your page target.

steps.title: Session 5: 45-minute reading sprint
steps.description: Set a 45-minute timer and read your page target. Hook: try to beat your page count from Session 1.

steps.title: Session 6: Read and explain it out loud
steps.description: Read for 40 minutes, then spend 5 minutes telling a friend or your phone's voice memo the most wild idea you read today.

steps.title: Session 7: Keep going to the home stretch
steps.description: Read for 45 minutes at your favorite time of day, with a snack as a reward. Done when you are within one chapter of the end.

steps.title: Session 8: Finish the last chapters
steps.description: Set a 45-minute timer and read to the final page, including the afterword. Done when you close the book and have read the last sentence.

steps.title: Capture your takeaways
steps.description: Set a 20-minute timer and write 3 big takeaways from Sapiens on your sticky notes or in your notes app. Done when you have three clear sentences and one rating out of 10.

grade.notes: Timing is a weakness: the student works on Today, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Monday, Wednesday and Thursday, so the plan ends on Oct 8 with only a 2-day buffer. Parent steps (the likely blocker) come late, and the parent text should be sent earlier. Step 2 on Today is a bigger lift right after the first step, and the first step still asks for a small decision (folder location).

plan.taskTitle: Submit the FAFSA for next school year
plan.analysis: Start with a tiny physical step, gather documents gently over a few days, then fill out and submit the form in short sessions with a buffer before October 10.

steps.title: Open the FAFSA site and make a folder
steps.description: Just open studentaid.gov in a tab and create a folder on your desktop called 'FAFSA'. That's it, you're done once both exist.

steps.title: Create or find your FSA ID
steps.description: Just log in at studentaid.gov with your FSA ID, or start creating one if you don't have it yet. Done when you can see your account dashboard or have the confirmation email pending.

steps.title: Gather your own documents
steps.description: Just collect your Social Security number, driver's license, and the last tax return and W-2s into your FAFSA folder (photos or scans are fine). Done when the files are in the folder, no need to read them.

steps.title: Ask about parent info and FSA IDs
steps.description: Just send one short text or email to your parent or guardian asking for their tax info and for them to create their own FSA ID if you're a dependent student. Done when the message is sent.

steps.title: Note your school codes and bank balances
steps.description: Just write down the federal school code for each school you're applying to (search 'Federal School Code Search') and jot approximate bank and investment balances. Done when it's on one note in your folder.

steps.title: Fill out the student sections
steps.description: Just start the form and complete your own sections: personal info, school selection, and your finances. Save and stop when those sections are finished.

steps.title: Complete the parent sections
steps.description: Just sit down with your parent and fill in their sections, using their tax documents and the IRS data transfer if available. Done when every section shows complete.

steps.title: Review and submit
steps.description: Just read through the summary page once, check names, SSNs, and school codes, then sign and hit submit. Done when you see the confirmation page.

steps.title: Save your confirmation
steps.description: Just download the confirmation page and drop it in your FAFSA folder. Done when the file is saved, then you can fully relax.

grade.notes: Total estimate (~3h 40m of steps) doesn't match the stated '4 hours 3 min', and Thursday has no specific times or deadline hour, so the schedule is vague about when to start and finish. The body-writing step also asks for 1 page total for two philosophers, which is tight, and the avoider tone is mostly low-pressure but could add more reassurance about stopping points.

plan.taskTitle: Write a 3-page essay comparing Plato and Aristotle on justice
plan.analysis: With only about a day left, the plan splits the essay into small, low-pressure sessions tonight and Thursday morning, finishing the writing early enough to leave time for a quick polish before it's due.

steps.title: Open a doc and paste in the prompt
steps.description: Just open a new doc called 'Plato vs Aristotle – Justice', paste in the assignment prompt, and type your name at the top. That's it, you're done once the page exists.

steps.title: Skim your notes on Plato's Republic
steps.description: Just look through your class notes or the reading on Plato's Republic (Books I-IV) and copy 3-4 lines about justice as each part of the soul and the city doing its own work. Don't worry about making them good, only paste them into your doc.

steps.title: Skim your notes on Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics
steps.description: Just glance at Nicomachean Ethics Book V and jot down 3-4 lines on justice as fairness, distributive vs corrective justice, and the idea of the mean. Paste them under your Plato notes.

steps.title: Write a rough skeleton
steps.description: Just type a one-line thesis guess and four bullet points: intro, Plato, Aristotle, comparison. A messy thesis like 'Plato sees justice as harmony, Aristotle sees it as fairness in practice' is totally fine.

steps.title: Write the Plato and Aristotle body sections
steps.description: Just write one rough paragraph or two on each philosopher, using your pasted notes as a guide. Aim for about 1 page total and permit yourself to write badly; you'll fix it later.

steps.title: Write the comparison and intro
steps.description: Just write one page: a paragraph on where they agree and differ (ideal city vs. practical fairness), plus a short intro and conclusion. Done means you've reached roughly 3 pages of rough text.

steps.title: Read through, tidy and submit
steps.description: Just read it aloud once, fix anything that sounds clunky, add your citations, and check the page count. Then submit it and take a well-earned break.

grade.notes: Step 7 is scheduled 'Tomorrow' (Thursday), which comes before problems 3-6 are done, so the sequence and timing break; the review step should land on Monday night or Tuesday. Thursday through Monday also leaves Saturday empty, and the first step could be tinier with less setup judgment.

plan.taskTitle: Finish 20 hypothesis testing problems in R
plan.analysis: Start with a tiny setup step, then work through the 20 problems in short sessions spread over several days, leaving a day for review before Tuesday's deadline.

steps.title: Set up your R script and paste in the problems
steps.description: Open RStudio, create a new script named 'hw_hypothesis_testing.R', and paste in the assignment's 20 problems as comments with a blank line under each. Done when the file is saved with all 20 problem headers.

steps.title: Skim the tests you'll need and note the R functions
steps.description: Look through your lecture notes or textbook chapter on hypothesis testing and write a cheat-sheet comment at the top of your script listing t.test(), prop.test(), chisq.test(), and any other functions the problems call for. Done when each test type has one example line.

steps.title: Do problems 1-5
steps.description: Write the code, run it, and type a one-line conclusion (reject or fail to reject, with the p-value) under each of problems 1-5. Done when all five run without errors.

steps.title: Do problems 6-10
steps.description: Work through problems 6-10 the same way: code, output, and a one-line conclusion for each. Done when all five are answered and the script runs top to bottom.

steps.title: Do problems 11-15
steps.description: Complete problems 11-15 with code, output, and a written conclusion. If one stumps you, mark it with 'ASK' and move on.

steps.title: Do problems 16-20
steps.description: Finish problems 16-20 with code, output, and conclusions. Done when every problem has an answer or an 'ASK' flag.

steps.title: Resolve flagged problems and check your work
steps.description: Go through any 'ASK' problems using office hours, a classmate, or the course forum, then re-run the entire script from a clean session to confirm there are no errors. Done when every answer states its hypotheses, p-value, and conclusion.

steps.title: Submit the homework
steps.description: Export or knit your work into the format your instructor requires and upload it to the submission portal. Done when you see the confirmation.

grade.notes: Timing is flawed: Oct 5 is a Monday, but Saturday is Oct 3, and the plan skips Monday's walk being tied to calendar setup order (the repeating event is created Sunday, after the walk it should schedule). Also, step 1 leash placement is fine but step 2 jumps straight to a 25-min walk today with no easing in; the plan treats a recurring habit as a one-week task with no ongoing continuation.

plan.taskTitle: Start your Monday/Wednesday/Saturday dog walk routine
plan.analysis: Since today is Wednesday, the first walk is today, so we make the setup tiny and warm, then build the routine by tying the next walks to Saturday and Monday.

steps.title: Put the leash by the door
steps.description: Just grab the leash and set it on the shoe rack or doorknob where you'll see it. Done when it's sitting by the door, nothing more needed.

steps.title: Take a gentle 20-minute walk
steps.description: Just clip on the leash, put on your shoes, and stroll around the block, with no pace or distance goals. Done when you're back home and your dog has had a sniff-around.

steps.title: Put Saturday's walk in your calendar
steps.description: Just add a 'Dog walk' event for Saturday at a time that suits you, like after breakfast. Done when it shows up in your calendar.

steps.title: Do Saturday's walk
steps.description: Just leave the leash by the door the night before, then walk whenever your calendar event comes up. Done when you've been out for about 20-30 minutes, and a short one counts too.

steps.title: Add Monday and Wednesday walks to your calendar
steps.description: Just create a repeating Monday, Wednesday and Saturday 'Dog walk' event at the same time you liked on Saturday. Done when the repeat shows up in your calendar.

steps.title: Do Monday's walk
steps.description: Just put the leash by the door and head out for an easy 20 minutes. Done when you're home, and your routine is officially rolling.

grade.notes: Step order is slightly off: the label and dose should be checked before the bottle is moved, and the first step has a minor decision (toothbrush or coffee maker). The plan also stops after three days, with nothing to keep the habit going beyond that, and the 20 min total doesn't match the step times.

plan.taskTitle: Start taking vitamins every morning
plan.analysis: Make the habit effortless by placing the vitamins where you'll see them, then plan the first dose and a quick check-in so it sticks.

steps.title: Put your vitamins next to your toothbrush
steps.description: Take the vitamin bottle and set it right beside your toothbrush or coffee maker, with a glass nearby. Done when you can see it from where you start your morning routine.

steps.title: Read the label and set your dose
steps.description: Check the label for the serving size and whether to take it with food, then jot the dose on a sticky note stuck to the bottle. Done when the note says exactly what to take and with what.

steps.title: Take your first dose with breakfast
steps.description: Right after you wake up, take the vitamins from beside your toothbrush with food or water, as the label says. Done when the pills are swallowed.

steps.title: Check the habit after three days
steps.description: Look at whether you took them Thursday through Saturday; if you missed any, move the bottle to where you'll hit it earlier, like next to your phone charger or the kettle. Done when the bottle is in a spot that worked.
